extracted.intended_audience: students/readers learning algebraic number theory (advanced undergraduates / contest trainees / beginning graduate students)
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter-level standards and procedures for working with rings of integers, ideals, and factorization in number fields: definitions, structural theorems (OK as Z-module, Dedekind domain), ideal arithmetic, factorization algorithm (Dedekind–Kummer), fractional ideals, ideal norm, and class group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matrix interpretation of multiplication-by-α (µα) and invariance of determinant/trace
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret µα : K → K (multiplication by α) as a matrix in any chosen basis of K/Q; the determinant and trace of µα do not depend on the choice of basis and satisfy det µα = product of conjugates = norm NK/Q(α) and Tr µα = sum of conjugates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick a convenient basis (e.g., {1, α, …, α^{n−1}} when appropriate) to compute the matrix; use minimal polynomial and Vieta relations to compute det (example and proof provided). This justifies multiplicativity of norms and additivity of traces (since µαβ = µα ◦ µβ and determinant is multiplicative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: ring of integers OK
rubrics_metrics.description: OK := K ∩ Z (the set of algebraic integers inside the number field K); equivalently, those elements of K that are roots of monic polynomials with integer coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this definition to restrict attention to the 'integral' subring of K; many structural theorems (Dedekind domain, module rank, etc.) concern OK rather than all of K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description/classification of OK for quadratic fields
rubrics_metrics.description: For K = Q(√d) (d squarefree): OK = Z[√d] when d ≡ 2,3 (mod 4), and OK = Z[(1+√d)/2] when d ≡ 1 (mod 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check by testing when an element a + b√d has minimal polynomial with integer coefficients; the exercise about 2a and a^2 − db^2 modulo 4 gives the exact criterion. Examples for d = 3, 5 are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property: every element of K is a rational multiple of an algebraic integer (K = Q·OK)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any x ∈ K there exists a nonzero integer n such that n x ∈ OK; i.e., every element of K can be written x = (1/n) α for some α ∈ OK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by considering the minimal polynomial of x or via the norm. This explains why denominators of elements in K can be cleared to land inside OK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion (Lemma 54.2.8): α is algebraic integer ⇐⇒ Z[α] finitely generated
rubrics_metrics.description: An element α is an algebraic integer if and only if the additive abelian group Z[α] is finitely generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward direction: a monic polynomial relation gives generation by {1, α, …, α^{N−1}}. Converse: finite generation by polynomials in α yields a monic polynomial satisfied by α (choose large N). Use this to test integrality by module finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic integers form a ring (closure under addition and multiplication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set Z of algebraic integers is closed under + and ×; in particular, for a number field K, OK is a ring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via finite-generation: Z[α] and Z[β] finitely generated ⇒ Z[α,β] finitely generated ⇒ Z[α±β], Z[αβ] are finitely generated subgroups, hence algebraic integers. This gives a practical route to show sums/products remain integral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure theorem: OK is a free Z-module of rank n
rubrics_metrics.description: If K has degree n over Q then OK ≅ Z^n as an abelian group; i.e., OK has a Z-basis of n algebraic integers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem (stated; proof deferred in text) allows thinking of OK as a lattice in R^{r1} × C^{r2}; used in finiteness arguments and Minkowski geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monogenic extensions and power bases
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension is monogenic if OK = Z[θ] for some θ (so {1, θ, …, θ^{n−1}} is a Z-basis of OK). Not all number fields are monogenic; some have index >1 between Z[θ] and OK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monogenic fields simplify computations (Dedekind–Kummer applies for all p); counterexamples exist (e.g., certain cubic fields). The index j = |OK : Z[θ]| matters in factorization algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: addition and multiplication of ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: For ideals a, b of a ring R: a + b := {a + b | a ∈ a, b ∈ b}; a · b := {a1b1 + · · · + anbn | ai ∈ a, bi ∈ b}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of ideal sum as generated by union of generators and product as generated by pairwise products; for principal ideals these coincide with element arithmetic ((x)·(y) = (xy)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal arithmetic via generators (Proposition 55.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If a = (a1,…,an) and b = (b1,…,bm) then a + b is generated by a1,…,an,b1,…,bm. (b) a·b is generated by the products a_i b_j for all i,j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to compute sums and products concretely in examples; product generators may be reduced using ideal membership relations (Euclidean/gcd-style simplifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: divisibility of ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: We say a divides b (write a | b) iff a ⊇ b (note reversed inclusion compared to elements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matches intuition: (3) divides (15) because (15) ⊆ (3); keep the inclusion reversal in mind when reasoning about divisibility of ideals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Dedekind domain
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral domain A is a Dedekind domain if it is Noetherian, integrally closed, and every nonzero prime ideal is maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three conditions together ensure ideal factorization behaves like integers. The key substantive condition is 'primes are maximal'; Noetherian and integrally closed are technical but used in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: integrally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: R (integral domain) is integrally closed if the only elements of its field of fractions K that are roots of monic polynomials with coefficients in R are the elements of R itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to check that OK is integrally closed; often shown by finite-generation arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: OK is a Dedekind domain (Proposition / Theorem 55.3.5–55.3.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any number field K, OK is Noetherian, integrally closed, and every nonzero prime ideal p ⊆ OK contains a rational prime p (hence is maximal). Thus OK is a Dedekind domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: use finite-generation / Z-module rank to show finiteness of OK/p (hence a field) and show a prime ideal contains a rational prime via norms; consequences: every nonzero prime is maximal and factorization of ideals is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique factorization of ideals in Dedekind domains (Theorem 55.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Dedekind domain A, every nonzero proper ideal a can be written as a finite product of nonzero prime ideals a = ∏ p_i^{e_i}, and this factorization is unique up to order. Divisibility corresponds to exponentwise inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outline uses existence of inverses for prime ideals, Zorn's Lemma for existence of factorizations, and uniqueness follows from primality properties; analogy to fundamental theorem of arithmetic is discussed along with required differences (no element-size measure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factoring algorithm / Dedekind–Kummer theorem (Theorem 55.5.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let K be a number field and θ ∈ OK with index j = |OK : Z[θ]| finite. For a rational prime p not dividing j, factor the minimal polynomial f of θ modulo p as f ≡ ∏ f_i^{e_i} (mod p). Then pOK = ∏ p_i^{e_i} where p_i = (f_i(θ), p) are prime ideals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe: (1) find f ∈ Z[x], (2) factor f mod p into irreducibles f_i, (3) define p_i = (f_i(θ), p), then pOK = ∏ p_i^{e_i}. If OK = Z[θ] (monogenic) then j = 1 and the theorem applies for all p. Use ideal norm to verify factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: fractional ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: A fractional ideal J of K (for Dedekind domain A with field of fractions K) is a set of the form (1/x)·a where x ∈ A and a is an integral ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently often one can represent fractional ideals as a/b for integral ideals a,b; fractional ideals let you form inverses and a multiplicative group analogously to Q for Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fractional ideals form a group; inverse and aa^{-1} = (1) (Theorem 55.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any nonzero integral ideal a, define a^{-1} = {x ∈ K | x a ⊆ A}. Then a^{-1} is a fractional ideal and a a^{-1} = (1). Nonzero fractional ideals form an abelian group under multiplication (identity (1)=A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show first for prime ideals then extend multiplicatively using prime factorization; this group JK (of nonzero fractional ideals) is central to defining the class group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal norm (Definition 55.7.1) and its properties (Lemma 55.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a nonzero ideal a ⊆ OK, the absolute (ideal) norm N(a) := |OK / a| (a finite positive integer). Properties: (a) N(a) is finite; (b) N(ab) = N(a) N(b); (c) if a = (α) is principal then N(a) = |NK/Q(α)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret N(a) geometrically as the covolume of the lattice a inside OK; it's multiplicative and extends to fractional ideals via rational exponents. Useful for size arguments (Minkowski) and verifying factorizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and role of class group ClK = JK / PK
rubrics_metrics.description: Let JK be the multiplicative group of nonzero fractional ideals and PK the subgroup of principal fractional ideals. The ideal class group ClK := JK / PK measures how far OK is from being a PID; its size (class number) is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ClK trivial ⇔ every ideal is principal ⇔ OK is a PID. Visualize classes geometrically (especially for imaginary quadratic fields: similarity classes of lattices). Finiteness of class number is a major theorem approached via Minkowski bounds later.
